back: Check: tcpdump port 179; ACL on either side · Fix: Open TCP/179; fix MD5 mismatch; verify correct source IP on multi-homed host

front: Symptom: Session flaps every ~60–180s — what do you check and fix?

front: Gotcha with BGP: what silently fails?
back: BGP alone won't save a bad IGP. If NEXT_HOP isn't reachable inside your AS, the route sits in RIB but never forwards.

front: When should you NOT use BGP?
back: Don't run BGP inside a single-site LAN — use OSPF/IS-IS; BGP's policy complexity isn't worth it. Don't announce prefixes you don't own (even "temporarily") — upstream filtering varies and leaks propagate globally. Don't expect sub-second failover from BGP timers alone — add BFD or track interface state.

front: What is IPFS (InterPlanetry File System)?
back: IPFS is a decentralized, P2P (Peer-to-Peer) file system that aims to make the we faster, safer, and more open. It allows users to store and share files in a distributed network of computers rather than relying on a central server. enables content-addressed file storage, mean…

front: What is Decentralized?
back: No central server stores the data. Instead, files are distributed across a network of nodes.

front: What is Content Addressing?
back: Each file is assigned a unique identifier (CID), generated based on its contents. This ensures the file’s integrity (i.e., it cannot be altered without changing its CID).

front: What is P2P Network?
back: Files are stored across multiple nodes in the network, and users can retrieve files from the closest available node, improving speed and reliability.

front: What is Versioning?
back: IPFS allows you to track and version changes in files, similar to Git.

front: What is File Duplication?
back: Files are only stored once across the network, reducing redundancy.

front: What is Half-open connections in one sentence?
back: One-line: TCP where one side has closed its write path (FIN sent) but the read path is still open — Stevens, TCP/IP Illustrated.

front: Explain the mental model of Half-open connections (how the system thinks).
back: TCP is full-duplex: each direction has its own FIN/ACK lifecycle. Half-open means one peer has shut down its outbound byte stream while the other can still send.

back: Inspect socket state — start with ss:

front: Symptom: CLOSE_WAIT count climbing on app host — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: ss -tanp state close-wait → owning PID · Fix: App not calling close() on accepted sockets after client disconnect; fix lifecycle / use finally blocks

front: Symptom: FIN_WAIT_2 pile-up on server — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: ss -tan state fin-wait-2 · Fix: Peer never ACK'd or never sent FIN; lower tcp_fin_timeout or enable tcp_tw_reuse where appropriate; fix client hang

front: Symptom: Connection "hangs" after server end() — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: tcpdump: FIN from server, no FIN from client · Fix: Client half-open; set { allowHalfOpen: false } or explicitly destroy() both sides

front: Symptom: LB shows healthy, app thread pool exhausted — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Compare LB idle timeout vs app socket timeout · Fix: Align timeouts; LB often 60s, app 300s → orphaned server-side sockets

front: Symptom: One direction works, other EOF unexpectedly — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: tcpdump -i any host <peer> and tcp[tcpflags] & (fin\ · Fix: rst) != 0

front: Symptom: Mass half-opens after deploy — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Spike in SYN-RECV or ESTAB without traffic · Fix: Rolling deploy + draining; old pods still hold connections; use graceful shutdown + SO_LINGER review

front: Gotcha with Half-open connections: what silently fails?
back: CLOSE_WAIT leak = application bug, not kernel bug. The remote side already closed; your process must close() the fd. Restarting the process "fixes" it temporarily — the leak returns.

front: When should you NOT use Half-open connections?
back: Don't enable allowHalfOpen: true unless the protocol explicitly needs unidirectional shutdown (streaming upload/download with independent lifetimes). Don't tune tcp_fin_timeout / tcp_tw_reuse without measuring — aggressive values can break legitimate long-tail responses.

front: What is Routing table in one sentence?
back: One-line: kernel data structure mapping destination CIDR → next hop; longest-prefix match wins — Kerrisk, Linux Programming Interface.

front: What is WebSocket in one sentence?
back: One-line: full-duplex framed messages over a single TCP connection, bootstrapped via HTTP Upgrade — RFC 6455.

front: Explain the mental model of WebSocket (how the system thinks).
back: WebSocket starts as HTTP/1.1 with an Upgrade handshake, then switches to a binary-framed protocol. No repeated HTTP headers per message — ideal for push, chat, live dashboards.

front: Symptom: 502 after ~60s idle — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: nginx proxy_read_timeout (default 60s) · Fix: Raise timeout; align with app heartbeat interval

front: Symptom: 504 on connect — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: proxy_connect_timeout; upstream down · Fix: Fix backend listen; check upstream block

front: Symptom: Random disconnects behind LB — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: LB idle timeout vs app ping interval · Fix: Send WS ping every (idle_timeout / 2); enable TCP keepalive

front: Symptom: Messages hit wrong backend pod — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: LB algorithm (round-robin) · Fix: Sticky sessions: ip_hash, cookie-based stickiness, or shared pub/sub backplane

front: Symptom: 403 / 400 Bad Request on upgrade — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: WAF blocking Upgrade header · Fix: Allowlist /ws/ path; disable request body inspection on upgrade

front: Symptom: SSL termination breaks WS — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Client uses wss://, origin uses ws:// internally · Fix: Terminate TLS at nginx; proxy to backend over HTTP with correct X-Forwarded-Proto

front: Symptom: Reconnect storm after deploy — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Connection count spike, CPU peg · Fix: Implement exponential backoff + jitter on client; drain old pods gracefully

front: Gotcha with WebSocket: what silently fails?
back: Default nginx 60s timeout is the #1 production WebSocket killer. Always set proxy_read_timeout explicitly.

front: When should you NOT use WebSocket?
back: High-frequency fan-out to millions of clients → dedicated pub/sub (MQTT, SSE, or managed realtime service) scales better operationally. Request/response CRUD → ordinary HTTP/REST or gRPC is simpler to cache, debug, and load-balance.
